meta.blurb: On a dreary November night, Victor Frankenstein's creation opens its eye, and Victor runs away. Alone, hungry and nameless, the Creature learns about people by watching them through a window. Then he comes looking for his maker, with a demand.
meta.bible: Robert Walton: an English sea captain sailing to the Arctic; he writes letters to his sister and meets Victor. Margaret Saville: Walton's sister in England, the person he writes to. Victor Frankenstein: the young scientist from Geneva who makes the Creature; clever, proud, and later full of guilt. The Creature: the being Victor makes, about eight feet tall, gentle at first, taught to be bitter by the cruelty of others; also called the monster, and he has no other name. Alphonse Frankenstein: Victor's father, a kind and respected man. Caroline Frankenstein: Victor's mother, who dies of scarlet fever. Elizabeth Lavenza: the orphan girl raised with Victor, later his wife. Ernest Frankenstein: Victor's younger brother. William Frankenstein: Victor's youngest brother, a child, killed by the Creature. Justine Moritz: the family's loving servant, wrongly accused of William's death. Henry Clerval: Victor's cheerful best friend. Professor Krempe and Professor Waldman: Victor's teachers at Ingolstadt; Waldman inspires him. The De Lacey family: a poor family in a cottage in the woods; the old blind father De Lacey, his son Felix and his daughter Agatha. Safie: a young woman from Turkey who joins Felix. Mr Kirwin: the Irish magistrate who questions Victor. Geneva: the home city of the Frankensteins, in Switzerland. Ingolstadt: the German university town where Victor studies. Chamonix, Mont Blanc and the Mer de Glace: the Alps where Victor meets the Creature. Orkney: the remote Scottish island where Victor starts a second creature. Evian: the lakeside town where Victor and Elizabeth spend their wedding night. Arctic: the frozen north where the story begins and ends. Strasbourg: the French city where Victor meets Henry. The Rhine: the river they sail down. Rotterdam: the Dutch port. London, Oxford, Windermere, Edinburgh, Perth: places on the English and Scottish tour. Ireland: where Victor lands. Cornelius Agrippa, Paracelsus, Albertus Magnus: the old writers Victor reads as a boy. Plutarch's Lives, The Sorrows of Werter and Milton's Paradise Lost: the three books the Creature finds. Thonon: where Victor finds Agrippa. Belrive and Plainpalais: places near Geneva. Secheron: the village where Victor stays when the Geneva gates are shut. Montanvert: the mountain above Chamonix; the Mer de Glace is the glacier. Justine's aunt lives at Chene near Geneva. Black Sea, Tartary, Russia: places of the chase. Voice and tone: serious, tragic and thoughtful; deaths are stated plainly with no gore; the Creature is sad and frightening in turn, never a joke; keep the framing of the story told by Victor to Walton.

beats.scene: Captain Walton writes at a desk in St Petersburg while snow falls outside
beats.summary: Robert Walton writes to his sister Margaret from St Petersburg, glad of the cold north wind and full of hope.

beats.scene: A boy reads old voyage books by candlelight in his uncle's library
beats.summary: Walton remembers how, as a boy, he read of polar voyages, tried to be a poet, and then chose the sea.

beats.scene: A young sailor hauls ropes on a whaling ship in freezing wind
beats.summary: He toughened his body and filled his mind with maths and science to prepare for a great journey.

beats.scene: Walton studies a map showing the white top of the world
beats.summary: He hopes to find a short sea road across the pole, a land of light, and the secret of the compass.

beats.scene: Sailors load a ship on a snowy quay at Arkhangelsk
beats.summary: At Arkhangelsk he hires a ship and a crew of brave men, though he still feels alone.

beats.scene: Walton leans on the ship's rail at dusk, thinking of Margaret
beats.summary: Walton tells Margaret he longs for a friend who would understand him, and promises to be careful.

beats.scene: The ship sails north between floating pieces of ice
beats.summary: The ship sails north through cold, bright days, and the first great pieces of ice appear.

beats.scene: A ship stuck in thick ice while a dog sledge passes far away
beats.summary: Fog and ice close in around the ship, and the crew sees a sledge driven by a huge figure.

beats.scene: Sailors help an exhausted, thin man onto the ship from a second sledge
beats.summary: Next morning a second sledge arrives, and a starving stranger is lifted on board.

beats.scene: Victor sits wrapped in a blanket as Walton listens beside his bed
beats.summary: The stranger recovers, becomes Walton's friend, and offers to tell his story as a warning.

beats.scene: Victor lies in a narrow ship's bunk, speaking quietly as Walton writes
beats.summary: Victor begins his story by describing his family, one of the most respected in Geneva.

beats.scene: A kind man kneels beside his dead friend's poor, silent family in Lucerne
beats.summary: Alphonse finds his ruined friend Beaufort dead and takes care of his daughter Caroline.

beats.scene: A young couple in wedding clothes stand outside a stone house in Geneva
beats.summary: Alphonse marries Caroline, and they create a loving home for their first child.

beats.scene: A mother walks by a blue Italian lake holding her small boy's hand
beats.summary: On a trip to Italy, the Frankensteins visit a poor family's cottage by Lake Como.

beats.scene: A fair-haired little girl sits among dark-haired children outside a cottage
beats.summary: Caroline sees Elizabeth, a golden-haired orphan, and decides to adopt her.

beats.scene: A small boy proudly watches a mother lift a little girl into a carriage
beats.summary: Caroline brings Elizabeth home as a gift for Victor, who calls her his own.

beats.scene: Two children and a baby play together in a sunny garden beside the lake
beats.summary: The children grow up together, gentle Elizabeth and fiery Victor, with little brother Ernest.

beats.scene: Two boys act out a battle with wooden swords in a garden
beats.summary: At school Victor makes a friend, Henry Clerval, who loves knights and adventure.

beats.scene: A boy reads a thick old book at an inn window in rain
beats.summary: At thirteen, Victor finds a book by Cornelius Agrippa, and his father calls it trash.

beats.scene: A boy watches lightning split an oak tree during a storm at night
beats.summary: He studies the old alchemists until lightning destroys an oak and he turns to modern science.

beats.scene: A young man packs books into a trunk beside a window in Geneva
beats.summary: At seventeen Victor prepares to leave for the university of Ingolstadt.

beats.scene: Elizabeth lies feverish in bed while Caroline sits beside her
beats.summary: Elizabeth falls ill with scarlet fever, and Caroline nurses her night and day.

beats.scene: A doctor leaves a bedroom while a worried family waits in the corridor
beats.summary: Elizabeth recovers, but Caroline catches the fever herself.

beats.scene: A sick woman holds the hands of a boy and a girl together
beats.summary: On her deathbed, Caroline asks Victor and Elizabeth to marry one day.

beats.scene: A pale woman rests quietly on a pillow in a candlelit room
beats.summary: Caroline dies calmly, and Victor feels the first dark void of grief.

beats.scene: Mourners in black walk behind a coffin through a Geneva street
beats.summary: After the funeral, Victor learns that death is real and the world goes on.

beats.scene: A girl in a plain dress sets a table for her grieving family
beats.summary: Elizabeth hides her sorrow, takes her aunt's place and comforts the family.

beats.scene: Two friends stand in a doorway while a stern merchant shakes his head
beats.summary: Henry Clerval's father refuses to send his son to the university.

beats.scene: Victor kisses Elizabeth goodbye at the gate while Ernest waves
beats.summary: Victor says goodbye to Elizabeth, his father and his brother.

beats.scene: A lone traveller in a carriage sees a white church steeple on the plain
beats.summary: He rides alone to Ingolstadt and sees its white steeple.

beats.scene: A stern short professor frowns at a nervous young student in a lecture hall
beats.summary: Professor Krempe mocks Victor's old books and tells him to start his studies again.

beats.scene: A pleased old professor smiles at a crowded chemistry lecture hall
beats.summary: Victor goes to Professor Waldman's lecture, which speaks warmly of the power of chemistry.

beats.scene: Victor and Professor Waldman talk in a study full of books
beats.summary: Waldman kindly advises Victor to study every branch of science, and Victor decides to follow him.

beats.scene: A young man bends over a laboratory table full of glass instruments
beats.summary: Victor works day and night and soon surprises the professors with his progress.

beats.scene: A lamp burns late over a desk covered with sketches of the human body
beats.summary: He becomes fascinated by the question of how life begins.

beats.scene: A student walks alone through a graveyard at night with a lantern
beats.summary: He studies the human body and the decay of death in vaults and graveyards.

beats.scene: A pale young man stares at his hands in a dim room
beats.summary: After months of labour, a sudden flash of understanding shows him the secret of life.

beats.scene: Victor dreams over a drawing of a tall, handsome human figure
beats.summary: He decides to make a new living being, and he imagines grateful children.

beats.scene: A hunched figure carries a heavy sack through an empty street at dawn
beats.summary: In secret he gathers materials from dissecting rooms and slaughterhouses.

beats.scene: A tall attic room with a smoking lamp, tools and unopened letters
beats.summary: He neglects his letters, his health and his friends as the seasons pass.

beats.scene: A thin young man works by candlelight in an attic, rain falling
beats.summary: On a dreary night in November, Victor's work is nearly done.

beats.scene: Rain streams down the window and a nearly burnt candle flickers over strange instruments
beats.summary: At one in the morning, he gathers his instruments around the lifeless body.

beats.scene: A huge yellow eye opens on a still, pale face in the candlelight
beats.summary: The creature opens a dull yellow eye, draws breath and moves its limbs.

beats.scene: A huge figure with yellow skin and watery eyes stands in the dim room
beats.summary: Victor sees how ugly the creature is, and his beautiful dream becomes horror.

beats.scene: A young man rushes out of a door and down a dark staircase
beats.summary: Victor runs from the laboratory to his bedroom and cannot rest.

beats.scene: A sleeping man dreams of a bright girl turning into a corpse
beats.summary: He dreams that he kisses Elizabeth, and she turns into his dead mother.

beats.scene: A huge figure holds a bed curtain and reaches toward a startled man
beats.summary: Victor wakes to see the creature beside his bed, and he runs away.

beats.scene: A man crouches in a wet courtyard at night, listening to every sound
beats.summary: He spends the night in the courtyard, afraid of every noise.

beats.scene: A pale man wanders through wet streets at dawn past closed shops
beats.summary: At dawn he walks through the streets, avoiding his own house.

beats.scene: A mail coach stops in a square, and a cheerful young man jumps out
beats.summary: At the inn, he meets Henry Clerval, who has just arrived from Geneva.

beats.scene: Victor stands laughing wildly at the door of an empty room
beats.summary: Victor finds his rooms empty, and the creature is gone.

beats.scene: A pale young man lies in bed while a friend sits close beside him
beats.summary: Victor falls into a long nervous fever, and Henry nurses him for months.

beats.scene: A thin convalescent looks from a window at green leaves in spring
beats.summary: Victor recovers slowly as the spring comes to Ingolstadt.

beats.scene: Victor reads a letter by the window while Henry watches kindly
beats.summary: Elizabeth writes a long letter with news of home, Justine Moritz and little William.

beats.scene: Henry holds a pen over paper while Victor, thin and tired, nods
beats.summary: Elizabeth begs for a few lines, and Victor writes to calm his family.

beats.scene: A friend carries glass instruments out of a room as Victor turns away
beats.summary: Henry removes the chemical instruments because Victor cannot bear the sight of them.

beats.scene: Two professors and two students stand in a lecture room, smiling politely
beats.summary: Victor introduces Henry to the professors, and Waldman's praise only hurts him.

beats.scene: Two friends study papers with Persian and Arabic letters at a table
beats.summary: Henry studies eastern languages, and Victor joins him in the work.

beats.scene: Two young men walk across green meadows on a summer day
beats.summary: Victor recovers further on long summer walks with his cheerful friend.

beats.scene: A young man breaks the black seal of a letter at a table
beats.summary: As he plans to go home, Victor receives a letter from his father.

beats.scene: A young man reads a letter with trembling hands while his friend watches
beats.summary: Alphonse writes that William is dead, murdered, and asks Victor to come home.

beats.scene: Victor rushes to a waiting carriage while Henry stands sadly at the door
beats.summary: Victor leaves at once, and Henry says a quiet, sorrowful goodbye.

beats.scene: A traveller stands outside closed city gates at night near the Alps
beats.summary: He reaches Geneva too late, and the gates are shut for the night.

beats.scene: A lonely man walks by a moonless lake near the place of William's death
beats.summary: He walks to the spot where William was killed and sees the dark Alps.

beats.scene: A great storm over the Jura mountains lights up the whole black sky
beats.summary: A powerful storm gathers over the mountains and the lake.

beats.scene: A huge figure stands in a lightning flash among trees on a hillside
beats.summary: In a flash of lightning, Victor sees the creature among the trees.

beats.scene: A drenched young man watches the dark hillside while the thunder rolls
beats.summary: Victor knows the creature killed William, but he cannot prove it or speak.

beats.scene: A family in black clothes meet in the hall of an old Geneva house
beats.summary: He reaches home and finds his father aged and Elizabeth in tears.

beats.scene: Elizabeth and Victor sit together by a fire as she tells her story
beats.summary: Elizabeth describes how William disappeared and was found dead the next day.

beats.scene: A family servant is led away by officers while others watch in sorrow
beats.summary: William's picture of Caroline is missing, and Justine is accused.

beats.scene: A crowded courtroom stares at a calm young woman in plain clothes
beats.summary: Justine's trial begins, and the crowd in the court already believes she is guilty.

beats.scene: A market woman points at the young servant while a judge listens
beats.summary: Witnesses say that Justine was out all night and that William's picture was in her pocket.

beats.scene: A young woman stands in the dock speaking quietly to the judges
beats.summary: Justine explains that she was at her aunt's house and then slept in a barn.

beats.scene: Elizabeth stands before the crowded court with her hands folded
beats.summary: Elizabeth tells the court that Justine is gentle and loved William.

beats.scene: Victor leaves the courtroom with a pale face, unable to bear the room
beats.summary: Victor knows the truth but cannot speak, because no one would believe it.

beats.scene: A stern priest leans over a frightened woman in a prison cell
beats.summary: The court finds Justine guilty, and a priest presses her to confess.

beats.scene: Victor and Elizabeth speak to Justine through the bars of her prison cell
beats.summary: Justine tells them that she gave a false confession to escape the priest's threats.

beats.scene: A gentle woman holds Elizabeth's hands in a bare stone cell
beats.summary: Justine says goodbye with calm courage and says that she forgives everyone.

beats.scene: A silent crowd gathers outside the prison on a grey morning
beats.summary: Justine is put to death, and Elizabeth weeps for the loss.

beats.scene: A lone rowing boat drifts across the dark lake under the stars
beats.summary: Victor drifts on the lake at night, thinking of his guilt and his family.

beats.scene: A grey-haired father gently touches the shoulder of his pale, silent son
beats.summary: Victor avoids everyone, and his father begs him not to nurse his grief.

beats.scene: A young man rides a mule along a mountain path beside a roaring river
beats.summary: Seeking peace, Victor travels alone to the valley of Chamonix.

beats.scene: A traveller looks up at huge snow-covered peaks above a green valley
beats.summary: The grandeur of the mountains and rivers lifts his heart for a short time.

beats.scene: A lone climber walks up a steep path in the rain, with mist below
beats.summary: In the rain, Victor climbs the steep path to Montanvert and sees the sea of ice.

beats.scene: A vast white glacier lies between two mountains under a clear blue sky
beats.summary: From the top, the view over the great glacier calms him a little.

beats.scene: A giant figure leaps across ice cracks toward a small, frightened man
beats.summary: A huge figure races over the ice toward him, and he knows who it is.

beats.scene: A furious man points at a huge, pleading creature standing on the glacier
beats.summary: Victor curses the creature, who asks him to listen.

beats.scene: A giant stands before a small man on the ice with his hands raised
beats.summary: The creature says that Victor owes him a maker's duty.

beats.scene: A small man lowers his raised fist while a giant waits in silence
beats.summary: Victor feels pity and curiosity, and he agrees to hear the creature.

beats.scene: A small fire burns inside a stone hut, and a giant sits beside it
beats.summary: They go to a hut on the mountain, and the creature begins his tale.

beats.scene: A huge figure sits alone in a dark room, confused by light and shadow
beats.summary: The creature describes his first hours, when light, sound and touch were all confused.

beats.scene: A giant in a stolen cloak walks away from a town at dawn
beats.summary: He leaves the house, finds a cloak and wanders out of Ingolstadt into a forest.

beats.scene: A giant drinks from a stream in a cold forest under a bright moon
beats.summary: Cold, hungry and thirsty, he drinks from a brook and sleeps under a tree.

beats.scene: A giant sits in a sunny glade and looks up at singing birds
beats.summary: He learns the sun, the moon and the birds, but his own voice frightens the birds.

beats.scene: A giant crouches beside a glowing fire left by travellers in the woods
beats.summary: He finds a fire, feels its warmth, burns his hand and learns to cook.

beats.scene: A frightened shepherd runs from a hut while a giant stands in the doorway
beats.summary: In a hut, a shepherd runs away in terror, and the creature eats his food.

beats.scene: Villagers throw stones at a giant running from a village in the dusk
beats.summary: In a village the people scream and throw stones, and he runs away hurt.

beats.scene: A giant crawls into a small, dry hovel pressed against a cottage wall
beats.summary: He finds a hovel beside a cottage and makes it his shelter.

beats.scene: Through a crack in a wall, a giant watches a girl carry a pail
beats.summary: Through a crack in the wall he sees a girl, a young man and an old man.

beats.scene: An old blind man plays a guitar while a giant listens in the dark
beats.summary: The old man plays music, and the creature feels his first pleasure.

beats.scene: A giant watches a family eat a thin meal through a wall crack
beats.summary: He sees that the family is poor and gives the best food to the old man.

beats.scene: A giant quietly leaves a bundle of firewood at a cottage door
beats.summary: He stops stealing their food, and at night he gathers wood for them.

beats.scene: A girl and a young man find a pile of firewood outside their door
beats.summary: The family finds the wood and wonders who has helped them.

beats.scene: A giant listens through a wall while a family speaks around a table
beats.summary: He learns that they speak with words, and he longs to understand them.

beats.scene: A young man teaches an old man's words with a finger to the lips
beats.summary: He learns a few words, such as fire, bread, milk and wood, and names of the family.

beats.scene: A giant looks sadly at his own reflection in a clear pool
beats.summary: He sees his own face in a pool and is horrified at what he sees.

beats.scene: Snow covers a cottage roof as the family huddles by a small fire
beats.summary: Through winter and spring he sees the family's sorrow and the love between them.

beats.scene: A dark-eyed young woman arrives on horseback at the cottage door
beats.summary: A young woman, Safie, arrives and is welcomed warmly by Felix.

beats.scene: A young woman and a young man bend over a book at a table
beats.summary: Safie learns French from Felix, and the creature learns it with her.

beats.scene: A giant sits in the dark with a book from the family's lessons
beats.summary: From the book the creature learns about history, wealth, families and war.

beats.scene: A young man tells a story to a dark-eyed woman by a fire
beats.summary: Felix tells Safie the story of her father, a Turkish merchant unjustly jailed in Paris.

beats.scene: A young man visits a prisoner through the bars and sees a veiled girl
beats.summary: Felix pities the prisoner, and he and the merchant's daughter Safie fall in love.

beats.scene: A hooded man helps an older man climb from a prison window
beats.summary: Felix helps the merchant escape, but the merchant secretly plans to break his promise.

beats.scene: A family leaves a French house with bags while officers stand by the door
beats.summary: The French court punishes the De Laceys, and the family is ruined and sent away.

beats.scene: A young woman and her maid walk a long road across Europe
beats.summary: Safie defies her father and travels to find Felix, and she arrives at the cottage.

beats.scene: A giant finds a leather bag of books beside a path in the forest
beats.summary: In the forest, the creature finds a bag with three books.

beats.scene: A giant sits in the hovel reading by the light of the moon
beats.summary: Plutarch, Werter and Milton's Paradise Lost teach him about heroes, sorrow and creation.

beats.scene: A giant reads old papers by moonlight, his hands shaking
beats.summary: In the pocket of his cloak, he finds Victor's journal and learns where he came from.

beats.scene: A giant weeps with his hands on his face in a dark forest
beats.summary: Reading about his making, the creature curses his maker.

beats.scene: A giant stands at the edge of the forest looking at the cottage
beats.summary: He decides to speak to the blind old man, whose eyes cannot judge him.

beats.scene: A giant stands trembling before a cottage door while the family walks away
beats.summary: One day, when the young people are out, the creature knocks at the cottage door.

beats.scene: A blind old man sits by a fire as a giant stands waiting
beats.summary: He speaks to old De Lacey, who welcomes him in kindly.

beats.scene: A blind old man gently takes a giant's hand in a warm room
beats.summary: De Lacey says that he will help, and the creature weeps with joy.

beats.scene: Three young people enter and freeze at the sight of a giant
beats.summary: Felix, Safie and Agatha return, and the family reacts with horror.

beats.scene: A young man strikes at a giant with a stick while a woman faints
beats.summary: Felix attacks him, and he flees, hurt and heart-broken.

beats.scene: A giant lies on the forest floor in rage, beating the ground
beats.summary: In his hovel the creature is furious and decides to take revenge.

beats.scene: A giant sets fire to a cottage at night with a burning branch
beats.summary: The family leaves, and he sets fire to the empty cottage.

beats.scene: A giant swims a freezing stream and carries a drowning girl to land
beats.summary: On his journey he saves a drowning girl, but a man shoots him.

beats.scene: A giant wounded in the shoulder walks through snow toward distant mountains
beats.summary: Wounded and angry, he swears revenge on all men and travels toward Geneva.

beats.scene: A giant reaches out toward a small boy playing in a green field
beats.summary: He meets William near Geneva and learns that the boy is Victor's brother.

beats.scene: A giant stands over a still small figure in a green meadow at dusk
beats.summary: Angered by the boy's words, the creature kills William, then takes the picture from his neck.

beats.scene: A giant bends over a sleeping young woman in a barn full of hay
beats.summary: He finds Justine sleeping in a barn and puts the picture in her dress.

beats.scene: A giant faces a small pale man in a stone hut
beats.summary: He tells Victor that he is lonely, and asks him to make a female like himself.

beats.scene: A small man shakes his head and backs away from a pleading giant
beats.summary: Victor refuses at first, saying that he will not create another monster.

beats.scene: A giant stands at the hut's door and holds out his huge hands
beats.summary: The creature argues that a companion would stop his anger and wickedness.

beats.scene: A giant points far away toward a map of distant forests and rivers
beats.summary: He promises that they will leave Europe and live far from all men.

beats.scene: A small man sits with his head in his hands while a giant waits
beats.summary: Victor sees that he owes him justice, and he feels the weight of his duty.

beats.scene: A small man holds out his hand while a giant bows his head
beats.summary: Victor reluctantly agrees, if the pair will leave the world of men forever.

beats.scene: A giant bounds away across a white glacier toward the setting sun
beats.summary: The creature swears to keep his promise and vanishes across the ice.

beats.scene: A tired man walks down a steep mountain path under a dark sky
beats.summary: Victor climbs down the mountain, exhausted, and goes home to Geneva in silence.

beats.scene: A grey-haired father speaks gently to a gloomy son in a lamplit room
beats.summary: Back home, Victor's father asks him to marry Elizabeth, and Victor says he must first make a journey.

beats.scene: Victor stands with maps spread on a table while his father listens
beats.summary: Victor says he needs a year in England, and his father agrees.

beats.scene: Elizabeth stands anxious at a gate as a carriage leaves Geneva
beats.summary: Elizabeth fears for him, and Victor sets out in secret dread.

beats.scene: Two friends in a small boat pass castles and vineyards on a wide river
beats.summary: At Strasbourg Victor joins Henry, and they sail down the Rhine.

beats.scene: Two young men look at a busy London street from a window
beats.summary: They sail from Rotterdam to London, where they stay for months.

beats.scene: Two travellers walk by a blue lake among green English hills
beats.summary: They tour England, from Oxford to the lakes.

beats.scene: Two friends stand on a hilltop above a Scottish town with a river
beats.summary: In Scotland, Victor says goodbye to Henry and goes on alone.

beats.scene: A small boat crosses a stormy grey sea to a bare rocky island
beats.summary: Victor sails to the far northern islands of Orkney and finds a lonely island.

beats.scene: A poor family leaves bread at the door of a tiny hut
beats.summary: He rents a small hut on the island, and the poor neighbours bring him food.

beats.scene: A pale man works alone at a table of tools in a dark hut
beats.summary: Victor begins his dreadful task, and every day he hates it more.

beats.scene: A thin man stares at his work in a dark hut, deep in thought
beats.summary: Victor fears that the new creature might be worse than the first, or that they might have children.

beats.scene: A huge face grins at a window; a man inside stares in fear
beats.summary: One night Victor sees the creature watching him from the window.

beats.scene: A man tears apart a half-made body as a giant howls outside
beats.summary: In horror, Victor destroys the unfinished female, and the creature howls with rage.

beats.scene: A giant stands in the hut doorway, pointing at a trembling man
beats.summary: The creature says, “I shall be with you on your wedding night.”

beats.scene: A man alone in a dark room listens to waves breaking on rocks
beats.summary: Victor sits alone in the dark, afraid, but still determined.

beats.scene: A small boat carries baskets of broken things out over a night sea
beats.summary: He puts the remains in a basket with stones and drops them into the sea.

beats.scene: A small boat tilts in a violent storm with no land in sight
beats.summary: A storm blows him away from the coast and out to sea.

beats.scene: A weary man on a boat sees green hills on the horizon at dawn
beats.summary: After many hours of danger, he sees the coast of Ireland.

beats.scene: Hostile townspeople stare at a strange man stepping from a boat
beats.summary: In the Irish town, the people stare at him with suspicion and anger.

beats.scene: A man kneels over a body on a stony grey beach
beats.summary: He is taken to see a murdered man, and he finds Henry Clerval's body.

beats.scene: A thin man wakes in a plain cell as a kind jailer brings water
beats.summary: Victor wakes in a jail after two months of fever, and Mr Kirwin treats him kindly.

beats.scene: A grey-haired father rushes into a small cell and embraces his thin son
beats.summary: Alphonse arrives from Geneva, and Victor is deeply glad to see him.

beats.scene: A magistrate reads papers while Victor sits quietly across the table
beats.summary: Victor learns that he is accused of the murder of Henry Clerval.

beats.scene: Orkney villagers speak in a courtroom as Victor listens with a pale face
beats.summary: Witnesses from Orkney prove that Victor was far away, and he is freed.

beats.scene: A man and his father stand on the deck of a ship at sea
beats.summary: Victor and Alphonse sail home across the sea.

beats.scene: Victor stares into the grey sea alone at the rail of a ship
beats.summary: On the voyage Victor thinks that he is the murderer of William, Justine and Henry.

beats.scene: A father and son talk in a carriage on a rainy French road
beats.summary: In France Alphonse worries about Victor's strange words and thinks they are a fever.

beats.scene: A man in a Paris room reads a letter from Elizabeth at a window
beats.summary: In Paris he receives a letter from Elizabeth, who asks if he loves someone else.

beats.scene: Victor stands alone at night by a window, thinking of the creature's threat
beats.summary: Victor decides to marry Elizabeth and to face the creature, whatever happens.

beats.scene: Victor writes at a desk by candlelight and seals a letter

A1A2: Captain Walton writes a letter to his sister from a cold city.
As a boy, Walton read books about brave men who sailed to the north.
He worked hard on a ship and studied many things to get ready.
Walton believes there is a warm, bright land at the top of the world.
In Arkhangelsk, Walton finds a good ship and hires strong sailors.
Walton feels lonely, and he wishes he had a friend to talk to.
The ship sails north, and soon the sailors see big pieces of ice.
Thick fog and ice stop the ship, and a huge man passes on a sled.
The next morning, a weak, thin man on a sled asks to come aboard.
The thin man gets better, and he says he will tell Walton his story.
Victor says his family is old and well known in Geneva.
Alphonse finds his poor friend dead, and he looks after his daughter.
Alphonse marries the girl, Caroline, and they have a happy home.
The family goes to Italy, and they visit a poor cottage by a lake.
Caroline sees a golden-haired girl, Elizabeth, with no parents, and she takes her home.
She gives Elizabeth to Victor as a present, and he loves her.
The children grow up together, and Victor has a little brother, Ernest.
At school, Victor makes a good friend, Henry Clerval, who loves stories.
At thirteen, Victor reads an old book about magic, but his father laughs.
One night, lightning hits a tall tree, and Victor learns about real science.
At seventeen, Victor gets ready to leave home for a big university.
Elizabeth gets a very bad fever, and Caroline looks after her day and night.
Elizabeth gets better, but then Caroline catches the fever too.
Caroline takes their hands and asks Victor and Elizabeth to marry one day.
Caroline dies in peace, and Victor feels a deep, dark sadness.
After the funeral, Victor sees that the world goes on without her.
Elizabeth hides her own pain and looks after the whole family.
Henry's father says no, and Henry cannot go to the university.
Victor says goodbye to Elizabeth, his father and his little brother.
Victor rides alone in a carriage and sees the tall church of Ingolstadt.
The first professor, Krempe, laughs at Victor's old books and is rude.
The next day, Professor Waldman gives a lecture, and Victor listens closely.
Waldman speaks kindly to Victor and tells him what to study.
Victor works day and night, and the teachers are surprised by his progress.
Soon he wants to know one big thing, the secret of life.
To learn it, he studies bodies and visits sad places at night.
After many months, Victor suddenly finds the secret that gives life.
He decides to make a new person, and he dreams of happy children.
He gathers what he needs in secret and hides it from everyone.
He forgets letters, friends and sleep, and the seasons pass by.
On a rainy night in November, Victor finishes his work at last.
At one in the morning, he gets ready to give the body life.
Slowly, the creature opens a yellow eye and begins to breathe.
Victor sees how ugly it is, and his hopes turn to horror.
He runs out of the room and cannot rest in his bed.
In a dream, Elizabeth turns into his dead mother, and he wakes in fear.
He wakes and sees the creature by his bed, so he runs away.
He spends the night in the courtyard, afraid of every little sound.
In the morning, he walks the wet streets and will not go home.
At the inn, Victor sees his dear friend Henry Clerval arrive in a coach.
Victor takes Henry upstairs, and he finds the room empty and is glad.
Victor becomes very ill with a fever, and Henry nurses him for months.
Slowly, as spring comes, Victor becomes strong again and sees green leaves.
Elizabeth writes a long letter about home and about little William.
Elizabeth asks for a few words, so Victor writes to calm his family.
Victor cannot look at his old tools, so Henry takes them away.
Henry meets the professors, and their kind words about Victor hurt him.
Henry studies the eastern languages, and Victor joins him with the books.
Victor grows stronger on long summer walks with his cheerful friend.
As Victor plans to go home, a letter arrives from his father.
Victor reads that William has been killed, and he must go home.
He rides away at once, and Henry says a sad goodbye.
He arrives at Geneva late, but the city gates are shut.
Victor walks beside the lake to the place where William died.
A great storm gathers over the dark mountains and the lake.
A flash of lightning shows a huge figure among the trees.
Victor knows the creature is the killer, but no one would believe him.
At home, Victor finds his father older and Elizabeth crying.
Elizabeth tells how William went missing and was found dead the next day.
William's picture of Caroline is gone, and Justine is blamed for it.
The trial starts, and the people in the room think Justine is guilty.
Some people say they saw Justine out all night near the place.
Justine says she was at her aunt's house, and then she slept in a barn.
Elizabeth tells the court that Justine is kind and loved William.
Victor knows who did it, but nobody would believe his strange story.
The court says Justine is guilty, and a priest tells her to confess.
Justine tells Victor and Elizabeth she lied about it to escape the priest.
She is calm and brave, and she forgives all the people.
On a grey morning, Justine dies, and Elizabeth cries for her.
At night, Victor takes a boat out on the dark lake alone.
Victor stays away from people, and his father asks him not to grieve.
To find peace, Victor travels alone to the valley of Chamonix.
The huge mountains and rivers lift his heart for a short time.
In the rain, Victor climbs a steep path and sees a sea of ice.
From the top, the view of the glacier makes him feel calmer.
A huge figure runs across the ice toward him, and Victor knows him.
Victor shouts at the creature, who only asks him to listen.
The creature says Victor made him and must be fair to him.
Victor feels pity and curiosity, so he agrees to listen to the creature.
They walk to a hut on the mountain, and the creature begins.
The creature says that at first he had no clear idea of anything.
He leaves the house, finds a cloak and walks away into a forest.
He is cold, hungry and thirsty, so he drinks from a brook.
He learns about the sun and birds, but his voice scares the birds.
He finds a fire and learns that it is warm and also hurts.
A shepherd runs from his hut in fear, and the creature eats his food.
In a village, the people scream and throw stones, so he runs away.
He finds a small shed by a cottage and decides to stay.
Through a crack in the wall, he sees three kind people.
The old man plays music, and the creature feels happy for the first time.
The family is poor, and they give the best food to the old man.
He stops taking their food, and at night he brings them wood.
The family finds the wood and wonders who has helped them.
He learns that they speak in words, and he wants to understand.
He learns some words, such as fire, bread, milk and wood.
He sees his own face in a pool and is afraid.
All through winter, he sees the family's sadness and their love for each other.
A dark-haired young woman, Safie, arrives, and Felix welcomes her warmly.
Safie learns French from Felix, and the creature learns with her.
From a book, he learns about history, families and wars.
Felix tells Safie her father's story, and the creature listens at the wall.
Felix feels sorry for the man in prison, and he loves his daughter.
Felix helps the man escape, but the man plans to break his promise.
The French court punishes Felix's family, and they lose everything.
Safie finds Felix after a long journey, and she arrives at the cottage.
In the forest, the creature finds a bag with three books in it.
The books teach him about heroes, sadness and how people begin.
In his cloak pocket, he finds Victor's papers and learns where he came from.
He reads about his making and curses the man who made him.
He decides to speak to the old blind man, who cannot see him.
One day, the creature knocks at the door while the young people are out.
He speaks to old De Lacey, who kindly asks him to come in.
De Lacey promises to help, and the creature cries with joy.
Felix, Safie and Agatha come home and see him with horror.
Felix hits him, so he runs away, hurt and heartbroken.
In his shed he is full of rage, and he wants revenge.
The family goes away, and the creature burns their empty cottage.
He saves a drowning girl on his journey, but a man shoots him.
Hurt and angry, he swears to take revenge and walks toward Geneva.
Near Geneva, he meets William, and he learns that the boy is Victor's brother.
The boy's words anger the creature, and he kills William and takes the picture.
He finds Justine asleep in a barn and puts the picture in her dress.
He tells Victor he is lonely and asks him to make a female like him.
At first, Victor refuses, and he says he will not make another monster.
The creature says a friend would stop his anger and wicked deeds.
He promises that they will leave Europe and live far from all people.
Victor sees that he owes the creature something, and the duty weighs on him.
Victor agrees, if the two will leave the world of men forever.
The creature swears to keep his promise, and he runs away over the ice.
Tired and sad, Victor climbs down the mountain and goes home in silence.
Victor's father asks him to marry Elizabeth, but Victor says he must travel first.
Victor says he needs a year in England, and his father agrees.
Elizabeth is afraid for him, and Victor leaves home full of fear.
At Strasbourg, Victor meets Henry, and they sail down the river Rhine.
They sail from Rotterdam to London, and they stay there for months.
They travel through England, from Oxford to the beautiful lakes.
In Scotland, Victor says goodbye to Henry and goes on alone.
Victor sails to the far northern islands and finds a lonely island.
He rents a small hut, and the poor neighbours bring him food.
Victor begins his terrible task, and every day he hates it more.
Victor fears the new creature might be worse than the first one.
One night, Victor sees the creature looking at him through the window.
In horror, Victor destroys the half-made body, and the creature cries out in rage.
The creature says, “I will be with you on your wedding night.”
Victor sits in the dark, afraid, but he does not change his mind.
He puts the broken parts in a basket and drops them into the sea.
A storm blows his boat far out to sea, away from the land.
After hours of danger, he sees the coast of Ireland.
In the Irish town, the people stare at him in anger and suspicion.
He is taken to see a dead man, and it is Henry Clerval.
Victor wakes in a jail after two months of fever, and Mr Kirwin is kind.
Alphonse arrives from Geneva, and Victor is very glad to see him.
Victor learns that people say he killed Henry Clerval.
Men from Orkney say Victor was far away, and he is set free.
Victor and Alphonse sail home across the sea together.
On the ship, Victor thinks he is the killer of William, Justine and Henry.
In France, Alphonse worries about his son's strange words and thinks it is a fever.
In Paris, Elizabeth writes to ask whether he loves another woman.
Victor decides to marry Elizabeth and to face the creature.
He writes that he has a secret and will tell her after the wedding.
Victor takes two pistols and a dagger, and the wedding is set for ten days later.
On a bright day, Victor and Elizabeth marry in the church at Geneva.
The couple sail across Lake Geneva toward Evian for the night.
At Evian, a storm rises, and Victor walks round the inn holding a pistol.
Victor searches the whole inn for the creature, and then he hears a scream.
He finds Elizabeth dead on the bed, and he falls to the floor.
Victor wakes and sees the creature at the window, and he fires but misses.
Victor brings Elizabeth home, and soon his father dies of grief.
Ill with sorrow, Victor decides that he must find and stop the creature.
The magistrate listens, but he does not believe Victor and does nothing.
At the graves, Victor swears revenge, and a cold laugh answers him.
Victor leaves Geneva at once and follows the creature across Europe.
In Russia, Victor finds messages that the creature has cut into trees.
The creature leaves food on his path, and Victor eats it with hate.
He walks on through the winter and sees his family in dreams.
Villagers say a giant went past them with dogs and a sled.
At the shore of the icy sea, Victor buys a sled and some dogs.
He drives over the ice, and sometimes he sees the creature far ahead.
The ice breaks, the dogs begin to die, and Victor cannot go on.
Victor sees a ship, and the sailors lift him on board.
Victor ends his story, and Walton shows him the pages that he has written.
Victor tells Walton to look for peace and not for glory.
The ice closes around the ship, and the sailors begin to fear.
The sailors ask Walton to turn south if the ice breaks.
Victor tells them not to turn back like cowards, but they do not listen.
The ice breaks with a roar, and Walton agrees to turn the ship.
Victor is too weak to go on, and he dies in his bed.
Walton hears a noise in the cabin and finds the creature beside Victor.
The creature says he hates himself, and Walton's anger melts.
The creature says he will burn himself and disappears into the dark.
B1B2: Robert Walton is writing to his sister Margaret from the snowy city of St Petersburg. The cold north wind blows on his face, and it fills him with joy and hope.
When Walton was a boy, he read every book about polar voyages that he found in his uncle's library. He tried to become a poet, but when he failed, he turned to the sea instead.
Walton worked on a whaling ship and slept on the hard ground to make himself strong. At the same time he studied mathematics and medicine so that he would be ready to lead a great journey.
Walton believes that near the pole there is a land of endless sunshine, and he hopes to find a short sea road to the East. He also wants to learn the secret of the compass, which nobody understands.
At Arkhangelsk, Walton hires a ship and a crew of brave, hard-working sailors. He is pleased with his preparations, but he still feels very much alone.
Walton tells his sister that he has no friend who shares his ambitions and could help him correct his plans. He promises that he will be careful, and he asks her not to worry about him.
The ship sails north day after day, and for a while the weather is bright and the wind is kind. Then the first great pieces of ice appear, and the sailors become quiet.
Soon the ice closes round the ship, and a thick fog hides the sea from view. When it clears a little, the crew sees a sledge pulled by dogs, driven by a figure of enormous size.
The next morning another sledge arrives, with only one dog left alive and one weak traveller on it. The sailors carry the stranger aboard, and Walton sees that he has suffered terribly.

The stranger is Victor Frankenstein, and after some days he is strong enough to speak. He and Walton become close friends, and Victor promises to tell him a story that may stop him from making the same mistake.
Victor lies in his narrow bunk and begins his story by telling Walton about his family. They are one of the most respected families in the city of Geneva.

Alphonse Frankenstein had a close friend named Beaufort, a merchant who lost all his money and hid in a small house. When Alphonse found him, Beaufort was dying, and he left behind a young daughter called Caroline.

Alphonse took care of Caroline until she was old enough to marry, and two years later they became husband and wife. They were very happy, and they gave their first child, Victor, all the love they could.
When Victor was small, his parents took him on a long journey to Italy, where they walked beside Lake Como. One day they stopped at the cottage of a poor family with many hungry children.

Among the dark-haired children, Caroline noticed a girl with golden hair who seemed to belong to a different world. Her parents had died, and the poor family had taken her in, so Caroline asked to bring her home.
The little girl was called Elizabeth Lavenza, and Caroline presented her to Victor as a pretty gift. He took the words seriously, and from that day he always called her his own.

Victor and Elizabeth grew up together as closely as brother and sister, though she was calm and he was full of fire. Later a younger brother, Ernest, was born, and the three children shared a happy home.
At school Victor met Henry Clerval, a merchant's son who dreamed about knights and daring adventures. The two boys became close friends, and they spent many afternoons acting out stories together.

When Victor was thirteen, the family stopped at an inn where it rained for days, and there he found a book by Cornelius Agrippa. He read it with delight, although his father glanced at it and called it trash.

Victor went on to read other writers who studied magic, and he dreamed of finding the secret of eternal life. Then at fifteen he saw lightning destroy an oak, and he began to turn towards real science.
When Victor is seventeen, his parents decide that he should go to the famous university of Ingolstadt. His bags are almost packed when a terrible misfortune strikes the household.
Elizabeth falls ill with scarlet fever, and her illness frightens everyone. Caroline refuses to let anyone else nurse her, and she sits beside the bed day and night until the fever finally breaks.
Elizabeth slowly recovers, and the family thinks that the danger is over. But Caroline has caught the fever herself, and the doctor's face already shows that there is little hope.

On the day she dies, Caroline calls Victor and Elizabeth to her bed and puts their hands together. She tells them that her greatest hope was to see them married, and she asks Elizabeth to be a mother to the younger children.

Caroline dies soon afterwards, quietly and without complaint, with her last look turned towards her family. Victor has never known such pain before, and for the first time he understands what it means to lose someone forever.

The funeral takes place in a grey morning, and then the world seems to go on exactly as before. Victor finds it cruel that people still laugh in the streets, since his mother has gone and cannot return.

Elizabeth is brave in her sorrow, and she hides her own tears so that she can comfort the others. She takes her aunt's place in the house, teaches Ernest and looks after the household with a calm, loving hand.

Victor's journey to Ingolstadt has been delayed by the illness and the funeral, but the day is finally fixed. Henry Clerval wants to go with him, but his father, a practical merchant, refuses to pay for a university education.
On the last evening, Victor says goodbye to his father, to Ernest and to Elizabeth, who has promised to write often. He kisses them one by one, and then he climbs into the carriage and rides away.

As the carriage rolls east, Victor thinks about the people he has left and feels very lonely. After several days he sees the white steeple of Ingolstadt rising from the flat country, and he steps out to meet his new life.

Victor's first teacher at Ingolstadt is Professor Krempe, a short, rough man with a harsh voice. When he hears that Victor has read Agrippa, he laughs and says that Victor has wasted his time and must begin again.

Victor leaves the lecture feeling hopeless, but a week later he goes to hear Professor Waldman speak about chemistry. Waldman is a kind man of about fifty, and he praises the scientists who have gained great power over nature.

After the lecture, Victor visits Waldman, who listens to his story without laughing. He advises Victor to study every part of natural science, and Victor leaves feeling that he has found a real teacher.

From that day Victor lives in the laboratory, working until late at night and sleeping very little. In two years he improves some of the instruments, and the professors are amazed by how fast he learns.

After a while, chemistry no longer satisfies him, and he begins to wonder about the beginning of life itself. He asks himself where the human body gets its spark, and he becomes impatient to know the answer.
To understand life, Victor decides that he must first understand death. For many nights he visits churchyards and the places where the dead are kept, and he watches how the body changes and decays.

After months of wild, hard work, a sudden light breaks upon him, and he sees how life might be given to something that has none. He is so excited that he almost cannot believe it, and he decides never to share the secret with anyone.

Victor decides to make a living being himself, and he plans to make it large so that the work will be easier. He imagines a new race of creatures that would bless him as their maker, and the idea fills him with pride.

To find the materials that he needs, Victor visits dissecting rooms and slaughterhouses, and he hates every minute of it. He carries his sad collection to a small room at the top of his house, where nobody can see it.
The work takes him through the summer and the autumn, and he hardly notices the beautiful weather. He forgets to write to his family, his health suffers, and he becomes thin and pale.
It is a dreary night in November, and the rain beats against the window of Victor's workroom. After almost two years of hard work, he is ready to see whether his creation will live.

At one o'clock in the morning, the candle is nearly burnt out, and Victor gathers the instruments of life around the body at his feet. His hands shake with anxiety, because he knows that the next moment will decide everything.
By the dim light of the candle, Victor sees the creature open a dull yellow eye. It draws a breath, and its arms and legs begin to move in a strange, shaking way.

Victor had chosen beautiful features for his creature, but now he sees yellow skin that hardly covers the muscles beneath it. The eyes are watery, the lips are black and straight, and the dream that he has worked on for years turns to horror.
Victor rushes out of the room, unable to bear the sight, and walks up and down in his bedroom for hours. He hopes that sleep will calm him, but his heart beats so hard that he cannot rest.

At last he falls asleep and dreams that he sees Elizabeth, healthy and beautiful, walking in the streets of Ingolstadt. When he kisses her, she turns pale and changes into the body of his dead mother, and he wakes up shaking.

By the faint yellow light of the moon, Victor sees the creature standing at his bed with the curtain in its hand. The creature's eyes are fixed on him, its jaw opens, and it makes a strange sound, but Victor runs out of the house.
He spends the rest of the night in the courtyard, walking up and down and listening for any sound. Every noise makes him afraid that the creature is coming for him.

When morning comes, rain is falling, and Victor wanders through the streets of the town without a purpose. He does not dare to return to his rooms, and he moves fast, as if he were running away from something.
At last he reaches the inn where the coaches stop, and he sees one arrive from Geneva. To his great surprise and joy, the person who steps out is his dear friend Henry Clerval.
Victor trembles as he climbs the stairs with Henry, afraid that the creature is waiting for them. When he opens the door, the room is empty, and he laughs and claps his hands in wild relief.

Henry sees his friend's strange laughter and becomes alarmed, because Victor is shaking and cannot speak properly. For several months Victor lies in a nervous fever, and Henry nurses him day and night without telling the family how ill he is.

In his fever Victor often shouts about the creature, and Henry believes that the words are only wild talk. Slowly, as spring comes, Victor grows well again, and one morning he sees green leaves outside his window.
As he recovers, Henry gives him a letter from Elizabeth, full of news about home. She tells him that little William has grown tall and sweet, and that the kind servant Justine Moritz is home again.

Elizabeth also writes that everyone is worried, and she begs Victor to send even a few lines to show that he is alive. Victor is too weak to write, so Henry writes a short note, and later Victor adds a few words of his own.
Whenever Victor sees a chemical instrument, his body shakes and he remembers the horror of that night. Henry quietly takes the instruments out of the room, and he is kinder than any brother could be.

As soon as Victor can walk, he introduces Henry to the professors of the university. Professor Waldman speaks warmly of Victor's talent, but his praise only makes Victor feel more guilty, because of what he has done.

Henry has no love for science, and he spends his time studying Persian, Arabic and Hebrew instead. Victor joins him in these gentle studies, and the beautiful poems of the East comfort him more than any medicine.

They spend the summer exploring the countryside around Ingolstadt, walking through meadows and along the river. The warm air and Henry's bright talk slowly bring back Victor's spirits, and he begins to enjoy life again.

Victor plans to go home to Geneva, but the autumn rain delays him, and then the cold weather turns the roads to mud. Just as he decides to wait until spring, a letter arrives from his father, and he breaks the seal.

His father's letter is very short, and every line of it is terrible. Little William, the youngest child of the family, has been found dead, murdered, and Alphonse asks Victor to come home as quickly as he can.
Victor hands the letter to Henry, who cries for the child he loved, and then Victor orders a carriage. Henry wants to help, but Victor must go alone, and they say a sad goodbye at the door.

The journey is long, and Victor feels both a wish to see his family and a fear of what he will find. When he reaches the city of Geneva at night, the gates are already closed, so he must stay in a village outside.
Unable to sleep, Victor walks down to the lake, to the place where his brother was killed. The dark shapes of the mountains rise around him, and everything seems peaceful and sad.
Over the Jura mountains, a great storm gathers, with heavy rain and thunder that echoes across the lake. Lightning lights up the whole sky, and the water looks like a sheet of fire.
In one flash of lightning, Victor sees a figure among the trees, near the hill of Salève. It is huge and twisted, and he knows at once that it is the creature he made.

The figure vanishes into the darkness, but Victor is sure that the creature murdered his brother. He cannot say so to anyone, because no one will believe a story about a monster, and they might think he is mad.
In the morning, Victor reaches his old home and finds that his father looks much older. Elizabeth, who was once so cheerful, is pale and full of tears, and Ernest cannot hide his sadness either.
Elizabeth tells him that William was playing with Ernest when he disappeared, and the family searched for him all night. In the morning they found him dead on the grass, with dark marks on his neck.
She adds that a small picture of Caroline, which William always wore, has disappeared. The police have found it in the pocket of Justine Moritz, the family's servant, and she has been arrested.

On the day of the trial, the court is full of people who have already decided that Justine is guilty. She sits quietly in her plain dress, and her calm face makes some of them whisper that she is cold.

One woman says she saw Justine near the place where William died, early on the morning after the murder. Another witness reports that the picture of Caroline was found in the servant's pocket, and Justine cannot explain it.

Justine tells the court that she spent the evening at her aunt's house outside the city. She came back after the gates had closed and slept in a barn, and she thinks the murderer put the picture in her pocket.

Elizabeth rises and speaks for Justine in a trembling voice, and she tells the court how kind and honest the servant has always been. She says that Justine loved William like a brother, and she asks the judges not to condemn her.
Victor listens in agony, because he knows that the real murderer is the creature that he made. He cannot tell anyone, since a story about a monster would only make them think that he is mad.
