She became the quiet centre of the household, and Victor watched her with a gratitude that deepened into something stronger.

Because of the illness and the funeral, Victor's departure for Ingolstadt had to be put off, but at last the day was fixed. His friend Henry Clerval had hoped to come with him, since the two had planned their studies together, but Henry's father was a merchant of the practical kind. He refused to waste money on what he considered useless learning, and Henry had to stay behind and take his place in the family business.

On the last evening, Victor said goodbye to the people he loved, and the parting was harder than he had expected. His father held him in a long embrace, Ernest begged him to return soon, and Elizabeth promised to write to him often and to wait for his coming home. He kissed them one by one, and then he climbed into the carriage and was carried away from everything he knew.

As the carriage rolled slowly towards Germany, Victor was left alone with his thoughts, and he felt the weight of his solitude for the first time. He had always lived among kind and affectionate faces, and now he would be a stranger among strangers, with no one to guide him. At last, after several days, he saw the white steeple of Ingolstadt rising from the flat plain, and he stepped down to begin a new life.

Victor's first meeting at the university was with Professor Krempe, a squat, gruff man whose voice was as unpleasant as his appearance. When he heard how many years Victor had spent on Agrippa, Albertus Magnus and Paracelsus, he declared that every moment had been wasted. He told the young man that he must begin again, from the foundations, with the books of modern science.

Disheartened, Victor thought of abandoning natural philosophy altogether, until a week later he happened to attend a chemistry lecture by Professor Waldman. The man was about fifty, with a benevolent face and a gentle voice, and he began by sketching the history of the science with a warmth that Krempe had never shown. The modern masters, he said, had performed miracles, for they had penetrated the recesses of nature and shown how she works in her hiding places.

After the lecture, Victor called on Waldman at his study, and the professor received him with a kindness that quite disarmed him. He listened to the whole story of the old authors without a trace of contempt, and he recommended a full course of study, from mathematics to every branch of natural science. Victor left the room with the feeling that he had found at last a true teacher and friend.

From that day, Victor's life was bound up in his work, and he spent his days in the laboratory and a large part of his nights over his books. Within two years he had made several improvements in the instruments of chemistry, and the university noticed his talent with respect and some surprise. His success only increased his appetite, and he looked for greater problems than any of his teachers had solved.

At length, chemistry alone no longer satisfied him, and his curiosity turned to the question that had always troubled his imagination, the origin of life itself. Where, he asked, does the human body find its spark, and why does that spark go out? The more he thought about it, the more it seemed to him the most wonderful mystery of nature, and the most impossible to leave alone.

To learn how life begins, Victor realised, he must first look closely at death, and he threw himself into the study of anatomy. For many nights he haunted churchyards and the vaults where the dead are kept, observing with an unflinching eye how the beauty of the human form fades and decays. He grew used to such sights, though he sometimes felt his nerves rebel and his mind shrink from what he did.

After months of exhausting labour, a sudden and brilliant light broke upon him, and he saw clearly the cause of the generation of life. He understood, to his own astonishment, that he might himself bestow animation on lifeless matter, and the discovery filled him with wonder and a dangerous pride. He tells Walton plainly that he will not reveal the secret, for he has seen where such knowledge led him.

Having found the means, Victor resolved to make a human being, and since the delicate parts were too difficult to work with, he chose to make it of gigantic size, about eight feet tall. He dreamed of a new species that would regard him as its creator, and of grateful children who would owe him their existence. Never once did he ask what would become of a being that had no parents and no past.

To gather the materials, Victor haunted the dissecting rooms and slaughterhouses, and though his whole nature protested, he forced himself to continue. He carried his gloomy collection away in secret to a solitary room at the top of his house, a kind of workshop where no servant or friend could see what he did. There, with the greatest secrecy, he began the work that would destroy his peace.

The summer passed, and then the autumn, and he did not see the beauty of the harvest or the vines, for his eyes were fixed on his task. His letters home grew rare, and his father's gentle reproaches went unanswered, while his own body wasted and his hands trembled. Yet something drove him on, and he later compared himself to a man who follows a path he knows he should not take.

It was on a dreary night of November that Victor beheld the accomplishment of his toils, after almost two years of labour that had cost him his health and his peace. The rain pattered dismally against the windows of his workroom, and the whole building seemed asleep. With an anxiety that almost amounted to agony, he prepared to find out whether his creation would live.

By one in the morning, the candle was nearly burnt out, and Victor collected the instruments of life around the lifeless thing that lay at his feet. His hands trembled as he worked, for he knew that the next few moments would answer the question that had occupied him for so long. A faint grey light fell across the floor, and he held his breath, unable to look away from the still, silent form.

By the glimmer of the half-extinguished light, he saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open, and he heard it draw a hard, laboured breath. A convulsive motion shook its limbs, and a kind of life stirred in the huge body that had lain so still. Victor, who had longed for this moment for years, felt his heart stop in his chest.

He had selected the features of his creature to be beautiful, with flowing black hair and teeth of pearly whiteness, and for a moment he had imagined a handsome being. Now, in the cold light, he saw instead yellow skin that scarcely covered the work of muscles and arteries beneath, and watery eyes set in a shrivelled face. The dream that had carried him through so many sleepless nights had vanished, and breathless horror and disgust filled his heart.

Unable to endure the aspect of the being he had created, Victor rushed out of the room and paced up and down in his bedchamber for a long time. He could not compose himself to sleep, and every sound within the house made his nerves jump like strings. His mind kept returning to the thing that lay in the room above, now alive and breathing.

At length, wearied out by anxiety, he fell into an uneasy sleep, and he dreamed that he saw Elizabeth in the full bloom of health, walking in the streets of Ingolstadt. Delighted, he embraced her, but as he kissed her lips they became livid with the hue of death, and her features seemed to change into those of his dead mother. He woke trembling in the dark, and a cold dew covered his forehead while his teeth chattered with fear.

By the dim yellow light of the moon, which forced its way through the window shutters, Victor saw the wretch standing by his bed, holding the curtain open. Its eyes, if they could be called eyes, were fixed on him, its jaws opened, and it muttered some inarticulate sounds, while a hand stretched out as if to hold him. He rushed from the house and ran down the stairs, and he did not stop until he reached the cold, open courtyard.

There he spent the rest of the night, pacing up and down in the greatest agitation and listening intently for the sound that might announce the approach of the demonical corpse to which he had so miserably given life. Each noise made him start, and every shadow in the yard seemed to him a figure coming to seize him. He was too frightened even to think, and he waited for the daylight as a prisoner waits for his judge.

When morning at last came, wet and cold, Victor walked through the streets of the town, passing the closed shops and the early workmen without really seeing them. He dared not return to his rooms, and he hurried on as if he wished to escape from the wretch whom he feared at every corner. His wet clothes clung to him, but he scarcely felt the cold or the discomfort of the long and sleepless night.

After walking for some time, he came to the large inn where the stagecoaches stop, and by chance he stood there at the very moment when one arrived from Geneva. As the door was thrown open, he saw Henry Clerval spring from the carriage, and a wave of joy rushed through him that was almost too strong to bear. After the horrors of that night, the sight of a familiar and friendly face felt like the sight of home itself.

With his heart beating wildly, Victor climbed the stairs of his house, half expecting the monster to be waiting for them at the top. He opened the door of his rooms with trembling hands, and to his joy he found that the creature was not there. He laughed and clapped his hands in a transport of relief, and the sound of that laugh was wild enough to alarm his friend.

Henry looked at him with growing fear, for he had never seen him so, and he supposed at first that some sudden madness had come upon him. Victor sank into a violent nervous fever that kept him in bed for several months, and during all that time Henry was his only nurse. He wrote to Victor's family that the illness was nothing, so that they should not be frightened by the news.

In his delirium Victor spoke wildly of the creature he had made, and Henry, who could not imagine any such being, took it for the ravings of an overheated mind. Slowly, however, the fever left him, and with the coming of spring his strength began to return, as the earth itself seemed to wake from sleep. One morning he saw the buds on the trees outside his window, and he felt a gentle happiness he had not known for a very long time.

As he grew stronger, Henry gave him a letter that had been waiting for him, written in Elizabeth's careful hand, and he read it with eager delight. She told him of the happiness of home, how his little brother William had grown tall, with blue eyes and dark lashes, and how brave and full of life he was. She spoke warmly of Justine Moritz, the young servant who had returned to the family and whom Caroline had loved dearly.

Elizabeth ended her letter by begging him to write, for his silence had made the whole household anxious, and she feared that he must be ill. She did not guess how near the truth she was, and Victor was moved almost to tears by her tenderness. As soon as his hand was steady enough, he sent his family a few lines to calm their fears.

The sight of anything connected with chemistry still gave him a violent shock, for it brought back to his mind that dreadful night. Henry, who guessed at his friend's feelings without understanding their cause, quietly removed every instrument from his rooms, and he never spoke of them again. No brother could have shown more gentleness, and Victor loved him all the more for it.

When Victor was well enough to go out, he introduced Henry to the professors, and the visit proved harder than he had expected. Professor Waldman praised his progress with a warmth that tore at him, for each kind word seemed to remind him of the monstrous use to which he had put his skill. He turned away with a sick feeling, and Henry, who noticed it, hurriedly changed the subject.

Henry himself had no taste for natural philosophy, and he devoted his time to the languages of the East, the glowing literature of Persia, Arabia and Hebrew. Victor, who was glad of anything that took his mind away from science, joined him in these studies, and they sat together over their books. The poetry of the East lifted his heart and gave him a consolation that no doctor had been able to supply.

The summer came, and the two friends spent many days exploring the beautiful country around Ingolstadt, along the river and across the sunlit meadows. Henry's lively talk and his delight in everything he saw were as good as any medicine for Victor, and little by little he became cheerful again. He walked and laughed as he had in the days of his childhood, and he almost forgot the weight upon his heart.

Victor had meant to return to Geneva in the autumn, but heavy rain and early snow made the roads so bad that he put off the journey until the spring. He settled down to wait, and for some weeks he lived in a kind of quiet peace, thinking only of the happy meeting that lay ahead. Then, one morning, a letter arrived from his father, and the moment he saw the black seal and the shaky handwriting he felt a stab of fear.

Alphonse's letter was short, and every line of it was a blow, for it announced that Victor's youngest brother William had been found dead, murdered by some unknown hand. His father asked him to come home with all speed, and he promised no more than that the family needed him. Victor read the words twice before he could understand them, and then he handed the page to Henry with shaking fingers.

Henry, who had loved the child, wept as he read, and he offered at once to go with his friend, but Victor insisted on travelling alone. He ordered a carriage and packed in a few minutes, and the two young men stood in silence at the door, too moved to speak. Then Victor pressed his hand and left, and Henry watched the road for a long time after the wheels had gone.

The journey seemed endless, for Victor was drawn by his longing for his family and held back by a horror of the news that waited for him. It was night when he approached Geneva, and he found the gates of the city already closed, so he was obliged to stop in a village a short distance from the walls. Unable to rest, he rose and set out on foot to see the place where his little brother had met his death.

The path led him to the shore of the lake, and in the dark he could just see the shape of the Alps and the pale gleam of the water. A storm was gathering behind the Jura, and in the stillness before it broke he felt a mournful peace, as if nature itself were thinking about the loss. He stood there for a while, with his hands clasped, and wept for the child he had loved.

Then the storm broke, with a fury that Victor had never seen, and thunder rolled and echoed from peak to peak across the whole valley. Lightning played over the surface of the lake until it seemed to be a sheet of flame, and the next moment all was blackness again. Victor watched it with a strange exultation, for the grandeur of the scene made his own sorrow seem both smaller and wilder.

In one flash, he saw a figure standing in the shadow of a clump of trees not far off, near the hill of Salève, and it stirred in the light. It was huge, deformed and unnatural in its gestures, and no human being could have been mistaken for it, so he knew at once who it was. The creature that he had made and abandoned was there, in his own country, and its presence on that night could mean only one thing.

A second flash lit up the hillside, but the figure had gone, and Victor stood alone in the rain, feeling certain that the creature was his brother's murderer. He thought of speaking, and at once he saw that it was hopeless, for a story of a living monster made from dead bodies would sound like the raving of a madman. So he kept silent, and the secret settled into his heart like a stone.

In the morning he came to his father's house, where he found that grief had aged the old man by many years. Elizabeth, who had once been the soul of cheerfulness, was pale and swollen with weeping, and little Ernest could not speak without tears. The household was heavy with a sorrow that no word could lift, and every empty chair was a reproach.

That evening, Elizabeth told him how William had gone out to play with Ernest in the fields near the town, and how the child had somehow slipped away from his brother. The family had searched until midnight with lanterns, and in the morning they had found the little body lying in the grass, with the marks of fingers on its throat. She said it with a calmness that cost her great effort, and Victor trembled to hear the words.

She added a strange and terrible fact, that the small picture of their mother, which William had always worn, had vanished from his neck. The police had later found it in the pocket of Justine Moritz, the servant whom everyone trusted, and they had arrested her on the spot. Elizabeth could not believe the charge, and she assured Victor that Justine was as gentle as a lamb and had loved William like a son.

The trial was held in a courtroom packed with curious faces, and Victor saw at once that the people there had already judged Justine in their hearts. She sat in a plain dress, pale but composed, and the very calm of her manner was held against her by those who wanted to see tears. A murmur of disapproval ran through the room, and nobody noticed how the girl struggled to be brave.

The first witness was a woman who swore that she had seen Justine near the spot where William died, at an early hour on the morning after the crime. A second testified that the miniature of Caroline had been found in the servant's pocket, and she held it up for the whole court to see. Justine, who had no idea how it had come there, could say nothing to explain it.

When she was allowed to speak, Justine told her story in a calm and steady voice, saying that she had spent the evening at her aunt's house, about a mile from Geneva. On her return the gates of the city were shut, and she had passed the night in a barn, and in the morning she had wandered about the fields in confusion. She suggested that the murderer had placed the picture in her pocket while she slept, but the judges clearly doubted her.

Elizabeth rose from her place and spoke in her friend's defence, with a voice that shook but did not break, and every ear in the room listened. She said that she had lived with the girl for years, that Justine had loved William as if he were her own, and that she could never have harmed him. Her words moved many in the room, but they could not outweigh the evidence that the court had heard.

Victor sat through the whole proceeding in an agony that no one could see, for he knew that Justine was innocent and who was truly guilty. A single word from him might have saved her, but he looked at the faces of the judges and knew that they would take it for madness. So he held his tongue, and that cowardly silence became the heaviest burden of his life.

In spite of everything, the court found Justine guilty, and the sentence was death, although even some of the judges seemed to feel troubled. Afterwards a priest visited her in prison and warned her, with great severity, that she would be cut off from the Church and from heaven unless she confessed to the crime. Frightened and confused, the poor girl at last gave way and said what he wanted to hear.

Elizabeth begged to see her, and Victor went with her to the prison, where Justine received them from a bed of straw with chains on her wrists. With tears running down her face, she told them that she was not guilty, and that she had confessed only to escape the priest's threats and to find a little peace. Elizabeth held her hands and wept, and Victor felt each word as a knife.

Justine, who had been so timid in life, met her fate with a courage that astonished them, and she told them that she was not afraid to die. She said that she forgave everyone, even those who had spoken against her, and she thanked Elizabeth for her kindness and her belief in her innocence. Then she said goodbye, and they left her in the quiet of the cell.

On the following morning, the sentence was carried out, and a silent crowd gathered under a grey sky to watch. Elizabeth wept in the house, and she said that she wished she had never been born, since the world had so much cruelty in it. Victor felt that he himself was Justine's murderer, and that the crime of the creature was also his own.

For some time afterwards Victor could find no rest, and in the evenings he would take a boat and row out on the dark lake alone. Under the cold stars, he sat and let the little craft drift, and the thought came to him that it would be easy to let the water end his suffering. But he remembered his father, little Ernest and Elizabeth, and he took up the oars and slowly rowed back to the shore.

In the days after Justine's death, Victor shrank from every human face, and he sat for hours in the dark with his own thoughts and his own guilt. His father, who saw how deeply he suffered, begged him gently not to feed his grief, since there were still living people who loved him and needed him. Victor, who could not speak of the cause of his misery, only bowed his head and promised nothing.

The house had become a prison to him, for every room was full of reproach, and he determined to find some peace among the Alps. He set out alone for the valley of Chamonix, riding a mule through country that grew wilder with every mile, and he hoped that the immensity of nature would quiet the storm in his mind. As he rode, the noise of the river Arve rose beside him like a constant, rushing voice.

The scenery of the valley was sublime, with mountains rising on every side and torrents falling from the heights, and for a short time the sight raised his spirits above the level of despair. He felt, for the first time in many months, something like a calm joy, as if the grandeur of the world proved that no single sorrow could be the end of everything. That night he slept deeply at the inn, but in the morning he woke to the sound of heavy rain on the roof.

In spite of the weather, he decided to climb the steep and difficult path to the top of Montanvert, and he went on foot, guided by the dull roar of the water. The rain made the rocks slippery and the mist hid the valley below him, but after several hours of effort he reached the summit and stood looking out. Before him lay a vast sea of ice, huge and silent, crossed by great fields of snow.

The view from the top took his breath away, for the glacier filled the valley between the two peaks, and its surface shone in the light that broke through the clouds. The enormous silence of that place made his own troubles seem as small as a grain of dust, and he felt a gentle, melancholy comfort. For a few moments, he forgot who he was and what he had done.

Suddenly he noticed a figure advancing toward him across the ice at a speed that no man could match, bounding over the cracks and ridges as if the glacier were a flat road. As it came closer, he saw that it was far taller than any human being, and a chill of terror ran through his body. Before the creature had reached him he knew it, and he felt a mixture of rage and fear that almost robbed him of his breath.

Victor burst out in a storm of fury, calling the creature a devil and a fiend and demanding that he go away, or else be destroyed. The creature stood quite still, and he said, in a voice that was steady though sad, that he had expected such a reception, since all men hated him. He asked only for one thing, that Victor should listen to what he had to say before he judged him.

The creature reminded Victor that he was his own creation, and that a maker owes a duty to the being that he has brought to life, as a father does to his child. He said that he ought to have been Victor's Adam, the first of a new race, but that he was instead like a fallen angel, driven from joy for no fault of his own. Then he asked Victor to make him happy, and he promised that he would again be gentle.

Victor sprang at him in a blind fury, trying to strike him down, but the creature easily avoided his blows and held him gently at a distance. Then something in the creature's voice reached his heart, and Victor felt a flicker of pity and a rising curiosity, together with a sense of the duty a creator owes. He lowered his hands and told the creature that he would listen to his story.

The creature led him across the ice toward a rough hut on the mountainside, where he lit a fire and invited Victor to sit down by its warmth. Victor, still trembling, took a place close to the flames, and the creature sat opposite him, huge and silent, watching the sparks climb. After a long pause, he began to tell the story of his life, and Victor listened.

The creature began by telling Victor that he could scarcely remember his first moments, for all his senses were confused and he could not tell light from sound or touch. Strange sensations pressed upon him from every side, and he did not know whether he saw, heard or felt them. It was a long time before the world began to settle into order, and even then he understood very little.

When he left the house in which he had been made, he found on the floor a cloak that Victor had left behind, and he wrapped it round his huge limbs. He wandered out of Ingolstadt without any aim, and he did not stop until he had come into a great forest, where the trees closed about him. There he sat down, exhausted, with no idea what he was or where he should go.

The cold troubled him, and so did the hunger and thirst that gnawed at him, though he did not at first know their names. By chance he found a clear brook and drank from it, and when he had slaked his thirst he lay down under a tree and fell asleep. He slept deeply and peacefully, with the soft sounds of the forest drifting about him through the long, cool night.

When he woke, a pale light was moving through the trees, and he looked up in amazement at the moon, which seemed to him like a guide in the dark. Little by little he learned the difference between night and day, and he listened with joy to the songs of the birds, which he longed to imitate. But when he opened his mouth to sing, a harsh and frightening sound came out, and the birds flew away.

One day, he came upon the embers of a fire that some wanderers had left behind, and he was delighted by the warmth. In his eagerness he thrust his hand into the flames and drew it back with a cry, astonished that the same thing could give such comfort and such pain. He quickly learned to feed the fire with wood and to cook the nuts and roots that he found, and he felt proud of his small discovery.

When food grew scarce, he followed a path out of the forest and found a hut where an old shepherd was eating his breakfast. The man looked up, uttered a shriek and fled across the fields at a speed that surprised his feeble limbs, and the creature stood motionless in the doorway, confused. Then he sat down and ate what was left on the table, and he thought that it was the best meal that he had ever had.

After a while he wandered into a village, and what he met there was far worse than the shepherd's terror. The children screamed and the women fainted, and the men, who had seized sticks and stones, drove him out with blows until he escaped across the fields, bruised and bleeding. He crouched in the open country, in misery, unable to understand what he had done to be hated like that.

At last he found a low hovel built against the wall of a small cottage, and it was a miserable place, but it was dry and out of the wind. He crept into it, thankful beyond words, and made up his mind to stay there until he was driven away, since he knew nothing about the people who lived in the cottage. For the first time he had a shelter, and he looked on it as a kind of home.

At dawn, a girl came out of the cottage carrying a pail, and the creature watched her closely through a chink in the wall, where there was a crack large enough to see through. A young man joined her, and the two were so gentle with an old man who followed them that the watcher forgot to be afraid. He saw that they were poor, and he saw that they were kind, and he did not move for hours.

That evening the old man sat down with a guitar and drew from it a sweet, simple music, and the creature, huddled in the dark behind the wall, listened with all his soul. It was the loveliest sound that he had ever heard, and it filled him with a gentle sadness and a gentle happiness that he had no name for. For the first time since his birth, he felt something that was not pain or fear.

Day after day, the creature watched the family from behind the wall, and he saw what the cottagers' life was like. They were poor, so poor that on some days they went hungry, and yet he noticed that they always gave the largest share of the food to the old man. This stirred his sympathy, and the more he watched, the more he felt that he loved them.

He resolved no longer to rob them, and he began to live on the nuts and berries of the forest instead, since he did not want to add to their hardship. At night, when they were asleep, he went out and gathered a large bundle of wood and laid it at the cottage door. He had never done a kindness before, and the sensation was strange and pleasing.

The next morning, Felix opened the door and found the pile of wood, and he stood for a moment in astonishment, looking all round. He went about his work, but the family talked about it all day, and nobody could guess who had been so generous. The creature, who watched from his hole, felt a warm happiness that he had never known.

He noticed that the cottagers used certain sounds that seemed to have a meaning, and that each sound was followed by a look or a gesture. He listened with growing eagerness, for he understood that these sounds were the key to the family's life, and that if he learned them he might one day speak to them. Often in the dark he tried to repeat the sounds under his breath, and he was clumsy at first.

After many days, he learned the names of simple things, such as fire, milk, bread and wood, and he also learned the names of the three people in the cottage. Felix and Agatha he heard called by name, while the old man was called father by them both, and he cherished these words as a miser cherishes gold. In this way, bit by bit, a window opened for him on the whole strange and moving world of human beings.

One evening, as he stooped to drink at a clear pool in the forest, he saw for the first time the reflection of his own face. He started back in horror, for he could not at first believe that the monstrous face in the water was his own, and when he was convinced he felt a bitter despair. At last he understood why people ran away from him, and why the cottagers would never love him.

All through the winter, he watched the little household, and he saw how often their faces showed sorrow, even when they tried to smile at one another. Yet he saw how deeply they loved, for Felix worked in the cold to support them, Agatha tended the house, and both were always tender to their blind father. Their goodness taught him what family might mean, and it made him feel his own loneliness more bitterly.

When spring came, a young woman rode up to the cottage on horseback, dressed in dark clothes and with a veil over her face. She had black hair and dark, gentle eyes, and when she took off the veil Felix greeted her with a joy so great that he could hardly speak. The creature later learned that her name was Safie, and he saw that the cottage had never been so happy.

Safie, however, did not know the family's language, and she spoke only in a strange, musical speech that nobody understood. So Felix began to teach her French every day, with a patience and gentleness that the creature admired, and the lessons took place at a table by the wall. Listening in the dark, the creature learned the words together with Safie, and he often learned them faster than she.

Through the lessons, the creature came to understand a good deal of what Felix read aloud from a book on the history of nations. He heard of the rise and fall of empires, of rich men and poor ones, and of the way that families and names passed from fathers to sons. He realised, with a pang, that he alone had neither father nor family, and he began to ask in earnest what he was.

One afternoon Felix told Safie the history of her own family, and the creature, crouching in his hovel, understood every word. Her father had been a rich Turkish merchant living in Paris, honoured by all until a court, for reasons of prejudice, condemned him in a trial that was manifestly unjust. He lay in prison, waiting for a sentence that was certain, and the news of his plight spread through the city.

Felix, who felt a generous pity for the man, began to visit him in his cell, and there he met the merchant's daughter, Safie. She was a lovely, gentle girl who had been brought up with hopes of freedom, and the two young people soon fell deeply in love. Safie promised that she would marry him, if only he could find some way to free her unhappy father.

Felix devised a plan, and one night, with a good deal of risk, he helped the merchant to escape from his prison and to hide until he could be taken from France. The merchant had promised to give his daughter to Felix in return, but he intended to break his word as soon as he was safe. He was a proud man, and he could not bear to give his child to a poor Christian.

When the French court learned that Felix had helped the prisoner, it punished the entire family with severity, and the De Laceys lost every possession they had owned. They were stripped of their money and their house, and they were driven out of France, and they came to live in a lonely cottage in Germany. Felix suffered most, because he blamed himself for the misfortunes of his father and his sister.

Meanwhile Safie's father had taken her away to Italy, and he told her that she must forget the poor young Frenchman, but she was resolved to be faithful. Slipping away from her father with only a maid for company, she travelled across Europe, and after many difficulties she found her way to the lonely cottage. Felix welcomed her with rapture, and the family had never been happier than on that day.

In the wood near his hovel, the creature found a leather bag that some traveller had dropped, and when he opened it he found three books. He took them back with him to his hiding place, and by the light of the moon he began to teach himself to read the pages. He was surprised at how swiftly the words came, because he had listened so long to the cottagers' lessons.

The books were Plutarch's Lives, The Sorrows of Werter and Milton's Paradise Lost, and each of them changed him in a different way. Plutarch showed him great men and noble deeds, Werter filled him with a gentle melancholy, and Milton made him think hard about his own creation. He felt like Adam, brought into the world alone, but he saw that Adam had been cared for by his maker, while he had been left to wander.

Then, one night, he remembered the cloak that he had taken from Victor's rooms, and in its pocket he found a bundle of papers. They were Victor's own journal of the months when he had made him, and the creature read them over and over, with growing dismay. Every detail of his making was there, set down in the cold language of science.

Reading Victor's description of the horror that he had felt, the creature understood that his maker had hated him from the very first instant. He cried out in grief and fury, for he saw that he had been made and then abandoned, and that no one on earth had wished him to exist. Cursed be the day on which he had been born, he said, and cursed be the hands that made him.

But as the days grew longer and warmer, his bitterness gave way to a kind of hope, and he began to think that he might win the family's love by kindness. He decided to approach the old blind father first, for a man who could not see his face might be willing to listen to his voice. Taking courage, he practised in the dark the gentle words that he would say, and he waited for a day when the others would be far from home.

One day, when Felix, Safie and Agatha had gone out to walk, the creature decided that the moment had come, and he went to the cottage door and knocked. A gentle voice called to him to enter, and he stepped inside with a heart that beat so loudly he feared the old man would hear it. This was the moment to which all his hopes and all his lessons had led.

The old man was sitting alone by the fire, and the creature explained in his best French that he was a weary traveller who wanted a little rest. De Lacey said at once that he was blind, but he welcomed the stranger with kindness and invited him to share the warmth. The creature sat down, struck with wonder that he should be received so gently.

Speaking carefully, he told the old man that he was friendless and that his greatest wish was to have a friend, and De Lacey assured him that he would do all that he could. The kind old man promised to ask his family to receive the stranger, and he said that in his experience a man was seldom wicked who longed for love. The creature, overwhelmed, wept with joy for the first time and took the old man's hand.

At that moment the door opened, and Felix, Safie and Agatha came in, laughing, and they stopped short in horror at the sight of the huge figure holding the old man's hand. Agatha fainted, Safie rushed from the room, and Felix sprang forward with a strength that astonished the creature. In an instant, all his hopes had turned to terror, and the warm room seemed to spin around him.

Felix tore him away from his father and struck him furiously with a stick, again and again, until the creature, who might have crushed him with one hand, gave way. His heart was broken, and he had no wish to fight those whom he had loved so long, so he fled from the cottage and hid in the forest. He was bruised in body and wounded in spirit, and no pain that the creature had ever known could be compared to it.

In his hovel that night, he lay on the ground and cried out with a rage that shook the whole forest, for the only beings he had ever loved had rejected him. He felt an overwhelming desire to destroy, to tear and burn, and he swore that he would never trust a human being again. It was then that the thought of Victor came to him, like a flame in the dark.

At dawn, he discovered that the family had packed their few possessions and left the cottage for good, and he understood that his visit had driven them away. In a blind fury he gathered some branches, set fire to the empty house, and stood in the dark watching until the flames had devoured it. Then he turned his back and went away into the forest to look for his maker.

His journey toward Geneva took many weeks, and he travelled mostly at night, avoiding all people and hiding in the woods by day. One day, as he crossed a river, he saw a young girl who had slipped and was being carried away by the current, and he plunged in and dragged her out. The man who ran up to her did not thank him, but fired a gun and wounded him in the shoulder.

The wound was painful, but the injustice of it hurt him more, for he had done a good deed and had been repaid with a bullet. Lying alone in the cold, he swore eternal revenge upon all mankind, and above all upon the man who had made him and abandoned him to such a life. Then he gathered what strength remained to him and walked on through the cold, empty hills toward the lake.

At last he came to the neighbourhood of Geneva, and one evening he saw a small, pretty boy running playfully through a meadow, and a thought struck him. A child, he told himself, was too young to have learned prejudice, and he might be able to make a friend of this one and be happy. He seized the boy, but William screamed and threatened him, and cried that his father was Monsieur Frankenstein.

The boy's cry of defiance roused the creature to a fury that he could not control, and in a moment he had seized the child by the throat. William lay lifeless at his feet, and as the creature gazed at his victim he saw a picture of a beautiful woman at the child's neck, and he took it. The sight of the lovely face gave him a brief moment of tender longing.

Searching for a place of rest, he came upon a barn, where a young woman lay asleep on the hay, and she was Justine. Filled with a sudden, bitter thought, he bent over her and slipped the picture into the folds of her dress, and then he ran out into the night. He knew very well, even as he did it, that this act would bring terrible harm upon the innocent sleeper.

With this the creature ended his tale, and he stood before Victor as a suppliant, his huge shape trembling a little in the firelight. He explained that he was lonely beyond words, and that he could not live among men, and he begged Victor to make him a female companion as deformed as himself. It was the only thing that could save him from despair, he said, and Victor alone had the power to give it.

Victor cried out that he would never agree, that nothing in the world could persuade him to create another being like the first, and that he would not let loose another terror upon the earth. He turned away in disgust, for the very thought of repeating his terrible labour made him feel faint. Yet the creature did not move or raise his voice, and he waited quietly beside the fire for Victor to calm himself and to listen again.

The creature answered that he did not wish to be cruel, that it was loneliness and the hatred of men that had made him wicked, and that he had once been gentle and good. A female of his own kind would not turn from him in disgust, he said, and with a friend beside him his rage would die, and he would be harmless. He asked only for what every living creature has, someone to share its life.

He promised, with solemn earnestness, that he and his companion would leave Europe forever and make their home in the vast forests of South America. They would live on nuts and berries, he told Victor, and they would never again trouble a single human being, nor would they ask for anything from the world. Their only wish, he said, would be to be left alone together in peace, far from the cruelty of the world.

Victor listened, and in spite of himself, he felt the force of what the creature had said, for he had made this being and had left him to suffer. He thought of the creature's unhappiness, of his tenderness among the cottagers, and of the cruel way in which he had been rejected, and he began to feel that he owed the wretch a duty. Justice, he believed, demanded that he do something to give his creature a measure of happiness, however small it might be.

At length, after a long struggle with himself, Victor said that he would consent, if the creature would swear that he and his mate would leave the neighbourhood of men for ever. The creature seemed overjoyed and promised it, in the name of the sun and of the blue sky, and he told Victor that he would watch over his labours. He added that when the work was finished, he would reappear, to take his companion away from Europe for ever.

The creature swore to keep his word, and then, as if he feared that Victor might change his mind, he turned and bounded away across the glacier with a speed that no man could match. Victor watched him until he disappeared among the rocks and ice, and then he heard, far off, the echo of a distant call. The sun was setting, and the long shadows of the mountains were falling slowly across the silent valley below the ice.

Victor descended the mountain path in the darkness, so weary that he could hardly set one foot in front of the other, and he reached the valley at midnight. The next morning he rode back to Geneva without speaking to anyone on the way, and he met his family with a pale face and a closed heart. He had promised to do a terrible thing, and he could not tell anyone why.

On his return home, Victor was gloomy and silent, and his father, who did not understand the cause of his grief, thought that a happy marriage might cure it. Alphonse proposed that Victor and Elizabeth should marry as soon as possible, and the young man heard the words with a cold feeling. He answered that he would gladly marry her, but he begged to be allowed first to make a journey.

He explained that he wished to spend a year in England, to study the latest discoveries of its scholars and workmen, and his father, who wanted only his son's happiness, agreed. The real reason, which Victor could not confess, was that he needed information that was to be found only there, in order to carry out his terrible promise to the creature. He felt that every day of delay was a danger, and that the creature was watching and waiting for him.

Elizabeth, who knew him better than anyone, saw that something weighed on his mind, and she feared that he was in danger and kept it from her. On the day of his departure, she begged him to write often, and she promised that she would wait for him, whatever the length of his absence. Victor kissed her gently and left Geneva with a leaden heart, knowing that he could not tell her the truth.

At Strasbourg, he found Henry waiting for him, for Henry had agreed to be his companion, and together they took a boat and floated down the river Rhine. They passed castles perched on the edges of high cliffs, green vineyards on the slopes and pretty villages along the shore, and Henry greeted every scene with delight. Victor, however, sat silent in the stern of the boat, thinking of the work that he had promised to do.

They crossed the sea from Rotterdam to London, where they stayed for several months, and Victor used the time to collect secretly the knowledge that he needed. Henry, who loved cities and crowds, filled his days with museums, libraries and conversations, and he tried to cheer his friend with his good spirits. Victor did his best to smile, but his thoughts were always with the unfinished labour that waited for him.

In the spring they left London and travelled slowly through England, stopping at Oxford and following the roads to the lovely lakes of the north. Victor noticed the fields, the hills and the clear water, and he admired the scenery, but the beauty could not touch the sadness within him. His whole mind was fixed on the dark task that lay before him, and he counted the days.

At last they came to Scotland, where an old acquaintance of Victor's family had invited them to stay for a time in the town of Perth. Victor felt that he could not continue any longer in company, since he needed to be alone in order to work, and he told Henry so, and begged him to forgive it. Henry accepted with his usual generosity, and they parted with an embrace and a promise to meet again.

Travelling alone to the far north, he took a boat to the Orkney Islands, which lie off the northern end of Scotland, and he looked for a place that was remote enough for his purpose. After some days, he found a small, bare island, where almost no one lived, and where the waves broke against the cliffs and the wind blew without mercy. It was exactly what he wanted for his secret labour, and the very thought of it filled him with a quiet dread.

On the island he rented a tiny hut with two rooms, one of which he turned into a workshop, and he settled there with a few tools and a few books. The poor people of the neighbourhood, who saw how thin and haggard he was, brought him bread and milk and clothing, and none of them asked what he was doing. He was grateful for their kindness, and he thought that it was more than he deserved.

He took up his labour again, and from the first day it seemed to him more horrible than it had been in Ingolstadt, for now he knew what he was doing. He would walk by the stormy sea for hours to quiet his mind, but whenever he returned to the hut, a sick feeling of disgust came over him. Day by day the dreadful task advanced, and day by day he hated it more.

As the days passed, Victor became more and more troubled by the work in front of him, and one evening he began to consider what he was really doing. The new creature might be gentler than the first, but she might equally be even more wicked, and she might refuse to live with him in exile. Worse still, the two of them might have children, and these children might spread over the earth as a race of devils.

He was sitting in the hut one night, lost in these dark thoughts, when he looked up and saw the face of the creature at the window, grinning. In that instant he understood that he had been following a madman's promise, and that he was about to create a being whose will he could not control. He sprang up from his chair with a cry of fury and fear, and the candle shook in his hand.

In front of the creature's eyes, Victor seized the half-finished body and tore it to pieces with his hands, scattering the remains over the floor. The creature gave a howl of despair and fury, a sound so terrible that it echoed along the cliffs, and then he withdrew into the night. For a moment Victor stood trembling, hardly able to believe what he had done.

After a while, the creature returned and came into the hut, and his face was dark with hatred. He told Victor that he had broken his promise and destroyed his only hope, but that he was still master, and that Victor would regret it. “I shall be with you on your wedding night,” he said, and then he went out into the dark.

Victor sat alone in the dark for hours, and he thought of the creature's last words and of the danger to Elizabeth, and a cold sweat came over him. Yet he did not repent his action, for he told himself that a man could not give in to threats and make the world a still worse place. He sat there without moving until the first grey light of morning crept slowly over the cold sea.

For two days after that, Victor stayed in the hut, hardly able to move, and then he gathered the remains into a basket and weighted it with heavy stones. At night he launched a small boat from the shore and rowed out some miles on the dark water, and there he sank the basket into the sea. Then he let the boat drift where the current chose, and he fell at last into an uneasy sleep.

Waking from his slumber, he found that a strong wind had risen, and the boat was being tossed about on the waves, far from any land. For many hours he fought against the storm, with the sail in tatters and the water pouring into the little craft, and several times he believed that his end had come. He was so tired and hungry that he hardly cared, and he almost wished for it.

At last, late in the night, he saw dim shapes of green hills against the sky, and as the morning light grew he realised that he was near the coast of a strange land. It was Ireland, as he learned later, and he steered the boat toward the shore with the last of his strength, giving thanks to heaven. He landed at a small town and walked up from the beach, weak and half-starved.

But the people of the town were far from welcoming, for they stared at him with suspicion, and some of them whispered and pointed as he passed. A man at last told him that he must go before a magistrate named Mr Kirwin, because a stranger had been found murdered on the beach during the night. Victor, confused and weak from the journey, did not understand what this could possibly have to do with him.

Mr Kirwin led Victor into a room where the body of a young man lay, and he asked him whether he knew the face. Victor looked, and he saw that the dead man had been strangled, and with a rush of horror he recognised the features, and he cried out that it was his dearest friend, Henry Clerval. Then his legs gave way beneath him, and he fell senseless to the floor of the room.

When Victor at last opened his eyes, he found himself in a bare prison cell, and he learned that he had been lying there delirious with fever for two months. The jailer who had looked after him was a gentle woman, and the magistrate, Mr Kirwin, came to visit him often and treated him with a courtesy that Victor had not expected. It was some days before he could speak clearly, and longer still before he could remember how he had come there.

One morning, he saw his father standing at the door of the cell, and tears ran down his face as the old man came forward and held him in his arms. Alphonse had hurried across Europe from Geneva as soon as he heard the news, and his face, lined by grief, showed what the journey had cost him. For a few moments neither of them could say a word, and the only sound in the cell was the old man's quiet weeping.

Mr Kirwin then told Victor why he had been arrested: a man had seen a boat come to the shore on the night of the murder, and Victor's was the only boat that resembled it. Henry Clerval had been found strangled, and the magistrate had been obliged to ask whether the stranger who had arrived at that very hour might have had some part in it. He spoke with great kindness and added that he wished to see justice done.

Mr Kirwin took care to find witnesses, and several fishermen and villagers from the Orkney Islands swore that Victor had been on his island, many miles away, on the night that Henry was killed. The court accepted their evidence without any difficulty, and the charge against him was dropped at once. Victor was free, though he felt no joy, for the real murderer was still alive and he was grieving for the best friend he had ever had.

Father and son left Ireland on a ship and sailed to Le Havre, and Victor, who was still weak, sat in a corner of the deck, huddled in his coat. Alphonse watched over him with such tender care that Victor felt he did not deserve it, and he tried to talk of home, of Elizabeth and of Ernest. His son answered only in short, tired words, and often he did not seem to hear what was said to him at all.

Standing alone at the rail, Victor looked at the grey waters, and his thoughts ran darkly through the faces of the people he had lost. He felt as if he were the murderer of William, of Justine and of Henry, and that every one of their deaths could be traced back to the hour in which he had made the creature. The guilt weighed him down, and he could speak of it to no one.

On the road through France, he broke into wild speeches about murderers and monsters, to the horror of his father, who could not understand a word. Alphonse concluded that the fever was still in his brain, and he begged him, with tears in his eyes, to be calm and to say no more. Victor fell silent at once, and he turned his face to the carriage window and watched the wet fields pass by.

At Paris, a letter was waiting for him from Elizabeth, and he read it at a window with a great swelling of the heart. She told him that she had heard of his illness and of his strange unhappiness, and that she could not believe it came from his sufferings alone. She asked him, with the greatest honesty and a touching gentleness, whether he had given his heart to another woman.

Victor read the letter and thought of the creature's words, “I shall be with you on your wedding night,” and understood that this was the hour when his enemy meant to strike. He decided that he would not be afraid, for if it must come to a fight, he would face it, and one of them would perish. If the creature killed him, it would at least be an end of his misery.

He sat down and wrote to Elizabeth that he loved her alone in the world and that no other woman had ever come between them, and that he would be glad to marry her at once. He added that he had one secret, so terrible that it would fill her with horror, and he promised to confide it to her on the day after the wedding. Then he sealed the letter with a trembling hand and sent it off by the next post, hoping that he would have the courage to keep his word.

Alphonse, delighted that his son had consented, fixed the wedding for ten days later, and the household began to prepare. Victor, meanwhile, prepared in his own way, for he put two pistols and a dagger in his coat, and he promised himself that he would not be taken by surprise. He did his best to appear calm so that Elizabeth would not suspect the dread that lay beneath.

On the morning of the wedding, Elizabeth was bright and radiant, and her happiness made Victor's heart ache, for he knew what he feared. They were married in the church at Geneva, in the presence of their friends and relations, and the congregation smiled at the bride, who looked more beautiful than ever before. Victor smiled too, though it cost him an effort that no one noticed, and his hand never strayed far from his coat.

After the ceremony, the couple embarked on a boat to cross the lake toward Evian, where they were to spend their first night together. The weather was perfect, and the great mountains rose above the water, and Elizabeth spoke gaily of the happy years ahead. Victor listened with a feeling of unreality, watching the sun sink behind the Alps and the shadows spread slowly across the surface of the lake.

At Evian the wind began to rise, and by evening dark clouds were moving over the lake, and the trees bent in the first gusts of a storm. Elizabeth, who was weary after the long day, retired to her room, and Victor kissed her and told her that he would join her soon. He then began to walk round the inn with a pistol in his hand, searching every corner for any sign of his enemy.

He passed through the passages and the courtyard and looked behind every door, but he found nothing, and he began to hope that the creature had not come after all. Just as he returned to the foot of the stairs, a piercing scream rang out from the room above, and he understood at once what the creature's threat had really meant. It was not his own life that was in danger on that night, but the life of the woman he had just married.

Victor rushed up the stairs and burst into the room, where he saw Elizabeth lying lifeless across the bed, with her head hanging and her face half hidden by her hair. He could only stare, and then everything went dark, and he fell senseless to the floor as if he had been struck. When he came to himself again, the people of the inn were gathered round him, and their faces were full of horror.

Remembering what he had seen, Victor rose and hurried back to the room, and there, through the open window, he saw the huge face of the creature grinning at him. The monster pointed with his finger at the body of the bride, and Victor drew a pistol and fired, but the figure sprang away and vanished into the dark. He rushed out and searched the shore, but there was no trace of him.

The terrible news was carried to Geneva, and Victor returned in a boat, with the body of Elizabeth, and he faced the family with a face of stone. Alphonse, who had already lost so much, was struck down by the blow, and he died a few days later, because his old heart could not bear this last grief. Ernest, the only one left, stood beside the grave, too young to understand fully, and too grieved to speak.

For a long time Victor lay in his bed, so ill with sorrow that he seemed to be half out of his mind, and he saw the faces of the dead pass before him in the dark. When at last he recovered enough to stand, a cold resolve came over him, and he decided that he must hunt down the creature wherever he had fled. All that remained to him was revenge, and he clung to it as a drowning man clings to a plank.

He went to a magistrate in Geneva and told him everything, beginning with the night in Ingolstadt and ending with the death of Elizabeth, and he begged him to help him find the creature. The magistrate listened politely, but his face showed that he took the story for the raving of a grieving man, and he said that no law could be applied to such a being. Victor left the house in a fury, and he swore that he would pursue the creature himself, alone, until one of them was dead.

On the night after the magistrate refused him, Victor went to the churchyard and knelt at the graves of William, Elizabeth and his father, and he raised his hands to the dark sky. He called upon the spirits of the dead to witness his vow of revenge, and he swore to hunt the creature until one of them died. As he finished, a loud and cold laugh echoed in the air, and a voice whispered that it was satisfied.

Victor rushed after the sound, but the shadow had vanished, and he knew that his search could begin nowhere but here. He left Geneva that very night and set off on the creature's trail, travelling through Switzerland and the south of France and on to the Mediterranean, where he took a ship to the Black Sea. At every stage he heard rumours of a monstrous figure that had passed a day or two before him.

In Russia and the wild lands beyond it, Victor began to find words cut into trees and carved on rocks, which the creature had left for him. They told him that the monster's reign was not yet over, that Victor must follow him to the far north, and that there he would find the end he sought. Victor read each message with a fury that kept him on his feet, and he never once doubted that the chase would end.

There were also gifts on his path, a loaf of bread laid on a stone or the carcass of a hare, for the creature did not mean his pursuer to die before the end of the chase. Victor ate the food with loathing, and he hated himself for needing it, but he knew that without it he would not have survived the journey. It was a bitter thing to be fed by his enemy, as though he were a beast being led to its own slaughter.

When winter came, he struggled on across the frozen plains, with the snow lying deep, his clothes in rags and his hunger a constant pain. Sometimes at night, when he slept in the open, he dreamed of his father, Elizabeth and Henry, and he seemed to see them smiling and pointing him onward. These dreams gave him the strength to rise again at dawn, to shake the frost from his coat and go on.

In a poor village by the northern sea, he questioned the people about the creature, and they told him of a gigantic figure who had passed a few days earlier with a sledge and a team of dogs. The man had frightened them, they said, and had taken their food, and then he had driven off to the north across the ice. Victor knew then that he was close, and he asked for nothing more than a fresh team of dogs and a few hours of rest.

At last he reached the shore of the Arctic Ocean, which lay frozen as far as the eye could see, and there he bought a sledge, a team of dogs and as much food as he could carry. The villagers warned him of the danger, but he took no notice, for every moment he delayed was a moment that the creature gained. He drove out onto the ice with a fierce and bitter joy, never looking back at the shore.

For days he drove across the great white plain, and from time to time, on the horizon, he saw a dark point that he knew was the creature's sledge. Sometimes the distance between them shrank to a few miles, and his heart would leap, and then a storm would hide the creature again. His hatred, which had once seemed a burden, was now the engine that drove him on.

But one day he heard a sound like thunder, and the ice began to crack, and a wide gap opened between his sledge and the creature, cutting him off. Little by little the sea broke up around him, and his food ran low, and one by one the dogs, worn out by hunger and cold, lay down and died. He was stranded on a floating field of ice, with the end close at hand.

As evening fell, through the mist he saw the dark outline of a ship caught in the ice, and he stretched out his arms toward it, though he had little hope. Walton's sailors, who had seen the strange sledge approach, came out to him, and they lifted his almost frozen body aboard and carried him to the cabin. So the tale that Victor had told ended at the place where it had begun.

When Victor had finished his story, he lay back, so exhausted that he could hardly raise his hand, and Walton sat beside him in awe at what he had heard. For some weeks, he had been writing each night what Victor told him, and he now showed him the manuscript, which Victor read slowly and corrected in places. He asked only that the truth be set down plainly, exactly as it had happened, without any softening.

Victor told Walton that he must not follow the same path, for he himself had wanted to be greater than nature allowed, and the result was ruin. The happiest man, he said, was the one who found his joy in a quiet life, and he begged Walton to seek wisdom and kindness rather than glory. Walton listened, with tears in his eyes, and promised that he would remember every word of this advice.

For several days the ship lay motionless, because huge mountains of ice had closed in on every side, and the crew could see no way out. The sailors were cold, hungry and discouraged, and as the days passed, many of them began to think that they would never see their homes again. Walton, who had dreamed of discovery for so many years, felt his own hope slipping away.

One morning a group of sailors came to Walton in the cabin, led by one of the oldest among them, and asked him to promise that he would turn south as soon as the ice broke. They were not cowards, but they did not wish to die in a land where no one would ever find their bodies, and they had families waiting in England. Walton, who could not refuse such a request, gave his reluctant word and watched them leave the cabin in silence.

Victor, hearing the noise, rose weakly from his bed and spoke to the sailors in a voice that was frail but steady, urging them to be men and not to turn back from a great purpose like frightened children. A few of the men were ashamed and stood with their eyes on the floor, but the rest remained firm, for their fear of the ice was stronger than any speech. Victor was helped back to his bed, tired and silent, while the sailors went on deck with their eyes cast down.

Not long afterward, with a sound like thunder, the ice began to split, and a clear channel opened through the frozen sea, and Walton, with a bitter heart, knew that his dream was at an end. He could not force the men to stay, and he did not wish them to die for his sake, so he gave the order to turn the ship toward the south. The sailors cheered, and the great white wall of ice slid slowly away behind the stern of the ship.

When Victor was told that the ship was turning, he accepted it without complaint, and he told Walton that he himself could go no further, for his strength was almost gone. His eyes were bright with a faint, strange light as he asked the young captain to seek happiness in tranquillity and to avoid ambition, even if it was only the apparently innocent one of distinguishing himself in science. A few days later he died, quietly, with the young captain sitting beside him.

Late that night, as Walton sat in his own cabin, thinking of all that had happened, he heard a strange sound coming from the room where the body lay, and he went in to see what it was. A gigantic figure was bending over the bed, with its face hidden by long, tangled hair, and one huge hand stretched out toward the dead man. When it heard him, it turned its head, and Walton, appalled by the sight, very nearly ran from the room.

But the creature looked at him with a face so full of sorrow that Walton's fear melted into pity, and the anger that he had meant to show went out of him. The creature said that he too had suffered, that he had killed the people whom Victor loved, and that he hated himself more than any man could hate him. Victor's death, he told Walton, was no victory but another stone upon his own heart.

He told Walton that he would leave the ship and go to the farthest north, where he would build himself a funeral pyre, and burn his wretched body so that no other being should ever be tormented by it. Then he sprang from the cabin window onto a raft of ice that lay close to the vessel, and the waves quickly bore him away. Soon he was lost in the darkness, and the silence of the frozen sea closed round him.
